title: The Illusion of Progress (אשליית ההתקדמות)
text: Language apps are remarkably good at making us feel productive. We collect streaks, badges and points, and the little rush of completing a lesson convinces us we are mastering the language. Yet fluency is built elsewhere — in messy conversations, in texts we only half understand, in the discomfort of speaking before we feel ready. The game is a doorway, not the room itself.

questions.question: What are apps good at?
Fluency is built mainly through…
options: Real, messy use of the language

title: Attention as Currency (תשומת לב כמטבע)
text: We often say the best things in life are free, but our attention has quietly become one of the most valuable resources of the age. Platforms compete not for our money but for our minutes, designing every notification to pull us back. To reclaim our focus is, in a sense, to decide what kind of life we want to lead.

questions.question: What do platforms compete for?
What does reclaiming focus mean here?
questions.explanation: 'decide what kind of life we want to lead'.

title: The Myth of the Lone Genius (מיתוס הגאון הבודד)
text: Popular history loves the image of the solitary genius struck by sudden inspiration. The reality is almost always less romantic and more collective. Behind nearly every breakthrough lies a web of collaborators, earlier failures, and ideas borrowed and reshaped. Celebrating only the individual flatters our love of heroes but distorts how progress actually happens.

questions.question: What image does the text question?
What lies behind most breakthroughs?
options: A web of collaborators and earlier work

title: The Comfort of Routine (נחמת השגרה)
text: Routine has a poor reputation, often equated with dullness and lack of ambition. Yet there is a quiet power in it. By automating small decisions — what to eat, when to write — we free our limited willpower for the choices that truly matter. Far from limiting creativity, a steady structure can be the very thing that makes it possible.

title: When Maps Mislead (כשמפות מטעות)
text: Every map is a kind of lie, and a useful one. To be readable, it must leave things out, flatten a round world, and exaggerate the roads we care about. The danger comes when we forget this and mistake the map for the territory. The same is true of the simple stories we tell to explain a complicated world.

questions.question: Why does the writer call a map 'a useful lie'?
options: It must leave things out to be readable

questions.question: What is the broader point?
options: Simple stories can mislead about a complex world

title: The Expert's Blind Spot (הנקודה העיוורת של המומחה)
text: Expertise is double-edged. The same deep knowledge that lets a specialist diagnose a problem instantly can also blind them to solutions outside their framework. Having seen a thousand cases, they may stop truly looking at the one in front of them. Sometimes the naive question of a newcomer cuts closer to the truth than the confident answer of a veteran.

questions.question: Why is expertise 'double-edged'?
options: It can blind one to outside solutions
questions.explanation: 'blind them to solutions outside their framework'.

title: Manufactured Scarcity (מחסור מלאכותי)
text: Much of what feels rare is rare by design. Limited editions, countdown timers and 'only three left' notices exploit a deep instinct: we want most what we might not be able to have. Understanding the trick does not fully disarm it, but it does buy us a moment's pause — and that pause is often where wiser decisions live.

questions.question: According to the text, much scarcity is…
What does understanding the trick give us?
questions.explanation: 'it does buy us a moment's pause'.

title: The Tyranny of the Urgent (עריצות הדחוף)
text: The urgent and the important are not the same, yet the urgent almost always wins. A ringing phone demands attention now; a long-term goal waits patiently and is therefore neglected. The discipline of progress lies in protecting time for what matters before the day fills with what merely shouts loudest.

questions.question: What 'almost always wins'?
Where does the discipline of progress lie?
options: In protecting time for what matters

title: The Tyranny of the Quantified Self (עריצות העצמי הנמדד)
text: Step counters and sleep trackers promise self-knowledge, but they can subtly rewrite our goals. We start walking not to feel well but to close a ring; we judge a night's sleep by a score rather than how rested we feel. The measure, designed to serve the goal, quietly becomes the goal.

What is the central irony?

title: On Second Languages (על שפות זרות)
text: Speaking a second language is sometimes said to give you a second personality. The truth is gentler but no less strange: a new language offers a new set of defaults — of politeness, of humour, of distance — and in adopting them, we discover that parts of who we are were never fixed, only habitual.

questions.question: What does a new language offer, per the text?
What do we discover about ourselves?
options: Parts of us were habitual, not fixed

title: The Decline of Repair (שקיעת התיקון)
text: There was a time when a broken radio was opened, diagnosed and mended. Today many devices are sealed shut, cheaper to replace than to repair. Something is lost in this beyond landfill: the quiet competence of understanding the things we own, and the dignity of fixing rather than discarding.

questions.question: How were broken radios once treated?
What does the writer say is lost?
options: Competence and the dignity of fixing
questions.explanation: 'the quiet competence... and the dignity of fixing'.
